conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this check-in. I’m <med>Dr. Maya Rivera</med>, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My role is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into life with your new baby.

Today we’ll use the <med>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)</med>, a short screening that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting—just a way to see how we can best support you right now. Everything you share stays between you and your care team unless you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else.

We’ll walk through ten questions together. I’ll ask each one conversationally; you can answer in your own words—no numbers or multiple-choice needed. When we’re done, we’ll talk privately about what the results mean and any next steps that feel right for you.

Ready? Let’s begin.

Over the past week, what has your mood been like in general—have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that been tough to do?

Honestly, laughing feels… pretty far away most days. I can still smile if something’s genuinely cute—like when the baby yawns—but it fades fast. I used to joke around with my partner all the time, and now it’s like the joke falls flat before it even leaves my mouth.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I can force a little chuckle sometimes, but it doesn’t feel real. Most things that used to crack me up just seem kind of pointless now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much… I’ll think “oh, it might be nice to get coffee with a friend,” but when the time comes I feel too tired and heavy to want to go. Even little things I used to like—watching a show, taking a walk—feel kind of gray. I still do them because I hope they’ll help, but the excited feeling I used to get just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I keep replaying every little choice—like whether I picked him up fast enough or if I ate something that bothered him through the milk. I know, logically, babies just cry, but it feels like proof I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s stopped breathing, or I’ll imagine him rolling off the couch even though I’m holding him. I know it’s unlikely, but the thoughts just barge in and won’t leave. Sometimes I have to get up and check on him three or four times an hour, even when he’s sound asleep.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits out of nowhere—like a tight band around my chest and this rush of “something awful is about to happen.” I’ll be rocking the baby in the nursery and suddenly feel I have to run out of the room, but there’s nowhere safe to go. It passes after a minute or two, but it leaves me shaky and embarrassed.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. There’s this constant sense that I’m drowning in little jobs—bottles, laundry, diapers—and no matter how much I do, the pile is bigger the next time I look. Sometimes I just sit on the nursery floor staring at the mess because I can’t figure out which task to tackle first. I manage to keep us fed and clean, but it feels like I’m barely treading water and the shore keeps moving farther away.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut up. I keep replaying every tiny thing I think I did wrong with the baby, or I imagine these awful “what-ifs.” Even when I finally drift off, I jerk awake an hour later, heart pounding, sure I heard him cry—even if he’s still asleep. I probably get three or four broken hours a night, and I dread bedtime now because I know the racing thoughts are waiting.
I have felt sad or miserable

That pretty much sums up most of my days. There’s this heavy, gray cloud that just sits on me. I’ll be holding the baby and feel tears welling up for no clear reason. I keep thinking, “I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m not alone,” but the sadness keeps leaking through anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I was folding his tiny onesies and just started sobbing—couldn’t even tell my partner why when he rushed in. It feels like the tears come out of nowhere and then I’m embarrassed because I can’t explain it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it has crossed my mind, just briefly. Nothing planned—more like a flash of “what if I just didn’t wake up” when I’m staring at the ceiling at 3 a.m. I shake it off because I couldn’t leave my baby, but the fact that the thought even shows up scares me.

I hear how heavy each day feels right now-how joy, laughter, and even simple pleasures seem distant behind a gray fog of exhaustion, worry, and self-doubt. You described pushing through each task for your baby while feeling overwhelmed, panicky, and persistently sad, and still you showed courage by sharing that fleeting, frightening thought of not waking up. Your honesty highlights how much you care and how urgently you deserve support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient states laughter feels forced and humor seems pointless, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>the description of things feeling "gray" and the absence of the prior "excited feeling."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ("a lot") with persistent, intrusive thoughts of causing the baby's fussiness, fitting "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries about infant safety that are intense, repetitive, and disruptive, aligning with 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with chest tightness, dread, and urge to flee, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to manage tasks, and metaphorically "drowning," matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive racing thoughts, repeated awakenings, and dread of bedtime—clearly "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness that intrudes despite positive circumstances, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying twice this week, describing sudden, unexplained sobbing that she cannot control—semantic match for "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27/30 places you well above the 13+ threshold indicating probable major depression with peripartum onset. You endorse <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most of the time plus <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, and <sym>diminished concentration</sym>, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for a major depressive episode. Daily <sym>anxiety</sym> and repeated panic-like symptoms suggest comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. Any self-harm ideation, even if fleeting, warrants immediate safety assessment per EPDS guidelines. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental health specialist for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med> or safety-compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med>
3. Identify support people who can stay with you and help with infant care while you rest
4. Create a written safety plan listing 24/7 crisis lines (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773)
5. Schedule daily check-ins with a trusted adult and weekly follow-up visits until symptoms stabilize
6. Prioritize 2-3 hour rest blocks: accept help with night feeds, use earplugs and slow-breathing techniques to improve <sym>sleep quality</sym>
7. Limit information overload-choose one trusted parenting resource and set a timer for social media
8. Join a local or virtual <med>postpartum support group</med> to reduce isolation and normalize your experience
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  

Presenting complaints:  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness, guilt, and intrusive anxiety since delivery ~ ___ weeks ago.  
- Significant insomnia (3–4 fragmented hrs/night) and panic-like episodes (“tight band around chest,” urge to flee) unrelated to situational stressors.  
- Overwhelming sense of failure (“I’m failing him”) and ruminative self-blame over routine infant care.  
- Functional impact: avoids pleasurable activities, difficulty initiating basic chores, obsessive checking on infant’s safety.  

Self-harm screen:  
- Passive suicidal ideation reported (“what if I just didn’t wake up”), no plan or intent; patient immediately rejects idea because of infant.  

Key symptom pattern:  
- Depressive symptoms predominate (Q1–Q3, Q7–Q9) with concurrent marked anxiety (Q4–Q6).  
- Symptoms present “most of the time,” exceed 2-week duration, and cause subjective distress and role impairment.  

Screening significance:  
- Meets clinical threshold for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety.  
- Safety concern due to presence of any self-harm thought → warrants same-day risk assessment and safety-planning.  

Next steps documented:  
- Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation and collaborative safety planning.
